title: Nature-Based Framework for Sustainable Architectural Design - Biomimetic Design and Biophilic Design
central_proposition: This paper proposes a comprehensive nature-based framework for sustainable architectural design by integrating biomimetic and biophilic design strategies, which are derived from natural systems, to achieve environmental, social, and economic sustainability and enhance human well-being.

concept_definitions.name: Sustainable architectural design
concept_definitions.definition: A set of rules and principles that conceives of the whole-building as an approach to design, construction, maintenance, and operations, aiming to solve environmental, social, and economic problems for providing resources and improving the quality of life for mankind.

concept_definitions.name: Sustainability
concept_definitions.definition: The endurance of biological systems to remain diverse and always productive, improving human life and well-being while preserving natural resources over a long time.

concept_definitions.name: Sustainable design
concept_definitions.definition: A philosophical basis for changing how building design, construction, and operation become more environmentally responsible and responsive to people, based on the sustainable triple bottom line principles (conservation of resources, cost efficiency, and design for the human).

concept_definitions.name: Biomimicry
concept_definitions.definition: The copying or imitation of the phenomena of nature or mechanisms of survival and environmental efficiency in manufacturing processes, acting as a sustainability concept in architectural design. It is a science that learns from nature as a model, judgment, and valuation.

concept_definitions.name: Biophilic design
concept_definitions.definition: The integration of design with nature, leveraging the human instinctive tendency towards nature, with physiological benefits focused on human health, well-being, and performance.

argument_structure: The paper first establishes sustainable architectural design as a response to environmental, social, and economic challenges, grounding it in the principle of sustainability derived from natural systems. It then introduces two primary nature-based strategies: Biomimetic Design (learning from nature) and Biophilic Design (integrating nature). Each strategy is detailed through specific aspects and methods related to resource efficiency, life cycle design, and human well-being. The paper culminates in a conceptual framework that visually links these principles, strategies, and methods, arguing for nature as the optimal source for achieving sustainability.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core causal logic is that nature, through millions of years of evolution, has developed optimal, sustainable solutions for resource management, energy efficiency, and ecosystem balance. By either directly mimicking these natural solutions (Biomimetic Design) or by integrating natural elements and patterns into the built environment (Biophilic Design), architectural design can inherit these inherent efficiencies and restorative qualities. Biomimicry provides mechanisms for clean technologies and resource conservation by replicating natural performance, while Biophilia leverages the innate human connection to nature to trigger physiological and psychological benefits, leading to improved health, well-being, and cognitive performance, alongside environmental protection.

findings.consequent: Solution of environmental, social, and economic problems, provision of resources, improved quality of life for mankind
findings.mechanism: It is a design approach that integrates these aspects as a set of rules and principles for the whole-building.
findings.quote: Sustainable architectural design is the design of the age. It is based on the solution of environmental, social and economic problems of architectural design for providing resources and improving the quality of life for mankind.

findings.mechanism: Natural systems embody the principle of sustainability and offer models for human benefit.
findings.quote: Sustainable solutions of architectural design result mainly from the principle of sustainability which is derived from natural systems and what they offer to humans.

findings.consequent: Mimicking nature's performance, provision of clean technologies
findings.mechanism: It is inspired from nature by implementing the Biomimetic design which mimics the performance of nature and provides clean technologies.
findings.quote: The first strategy is inspired from nature by implementing the Biomimetic design which mimics the performance of nature and provides clean technologies.

findings.mechanism: It is integrated into nature by using Biophilic design and its role in achieving human well-being and improving their performance.
findings.quote: The second strategy is integrated into nature by using Biophilic design and its role in achieving human well-being and improving their performance.

findings.antecedent: Application of biophilia and biomimicry concepts in design, construction, and maintenance of buildings
findings.mechanism: Biomimicry provides models for resource efficiency, while Biophilia enhances human interaction and well-being, both contributing to sustainability.
findings.quote: Thus, the application of biophia and biomimicry concepts in design, construction and maintenance of buildings achieves the principles of sustainability in the project.

findings.mechanism: Nature is based on the principle of sustainability, embodying optimal design (nothing missing or unnecessary) that humans cannot match.
findings.quote: Since nature is based on the principle of sustainability, the accuracy of the human will never match the beauty, simplicity or directness of nature; where there is nothing missing or is not necessary as it is the optimal design.

findings.mechanism: By implementing nature's principles (e.g., sunlight-based, energy-efficient, recycling, diversity) in daily design solutions.
findings.quote: Thus, learning from nature provides us with the methods that must be implemented in daily design solutions through Biomimetic design to create sustainable societies as nature does.

findings.consequent: Therapeutic benefits, positive effects on human health and well-being
findings.mechanism: Nature provides restorative qualities that positively impact human health and well-being.
findings.quote: In the literature of environmental psychology, the potential therapeutic benefits and positive effects on human health and wellbeing by exposure to nature environments were studied by Stephen Kellert and Elizabeth Calabrese in document “The Practice of Biophilic Design".

findings.mechanism: Simulating living organisms' methods to conserve resources in terms of form, material, construction, process, and function.
findings.quote: These aspects are derived from simulating living organisms to access different design methods to conserve resources (energy, water and materials).

findings.antecedent: Nature into the built-environment strategies (Biophilic design)
findings.mechanism: Integrating natural elements (ventilation, lighting, shapes, products, landscapes) to create restorative environments and preserve the environment.
findings.quote: Therefore, the buildings and living spaces of biophilic design include the basic elements from natural ventilation and natural lighting to natural shapes, products and landscapes and all that makes people feel that they are in a natural environment.

findings.antecedent: Biomimetic design (simulating nature's methods for ventilation, lighting, insulation, and forms)
findings.consequent: Reduced energy consumption, comfortable temperature levels
findings.mechanism: Mimicking natural forms and processes that optimize energy use and thermal regulation, such as natural ventilation, lighting, and insulation methods.
findings.quote: First, (Table 1) illustrates the reduction of energy consumption by ventilation and natural lighting methods and keeping comfortable temperature levels by way of insulation methods and using natural forms to interact with the surrounding environment [11].

findings.consequent: Preserved materials (more durable, less maintenance, environmentally responsive)
findings.mechanism: Mimicking natural material properties for durability, low maintenance, and environmental interaction (e.g., localized, environment-friendly, long-lasting materials).
findings.quote: Second, it illustrates preserving materials by using localized materials, environment friendly forms, and long lasting materials which simulates natural materials in terms of being more durable, require less maintenance and deal with the surrounding environment.

findings.antecedent: Biomimetic design (simulating nature's water conservation methods)
findings.mechanism: Mimicking natural processes for water collection and surface properties (e.g., manufacturing surfaces, harvesting, collecting water, designing water collecting devices).
findings.quote: Third, it shows how water conservation is carried out by simulating nature methods of manufacturing surfaces, harvesting, collecting water, or designing water collecting devices.

findings.antecedent: Biomimicry in Life Cycle Design (mimicking natural systems)
findings.consequent: Optimum consumption of resources, zero waste
findings.mechanism: Natural systems operate in closed loops, using resources for the longest possible period and recovering/refurbishing to eliminate waste.
findings.quote: The large number of organisms form an industrial network that mimics the systems of nature and produces a large amount of useful outputs as inputs where the resources move to zero waste ways.

findings.antecedent: Biomimicry in Life Cycle Design (simulating plants, insects, birds)
findings.consequent: Prevention of environmental pollution (anti-bacterial, anti-fogging, anti-corrosion, CO2 reduction, harmful emissions prevention)
findings.mechanism: Mimicking natural surfaces and processes that have self-cleaning, protective, or filtering properties.
findings.quote: Resource Management: It is the prevention of environmental pollution through application of surfaces to prevent pollution, anti-bacterial, anti-fogging and anti-corrosion, reducing CO2 emissions, preventing harmful emissions by simulating plants, insects and birds.

findings.antecedent: Biophilic design elements (green areas, trees, green roofs, green walls)
findings.consequent: Environmental preservation (energy saving, water conservation, filtration, phytoremediation, carbon reduction, biodiversity)
findings.mechanism: These elements directly contribute to ecological functions such as reducing urban heat island effect, adjusting local climate, improving thermal behavior, reducing rainwater flow, purifying water, and sequestering carbon.
findings.quote: The elements of the biophilic design; green areas, trees, green roofs, green walls...etc, have an important role in preserving the environment by energy saving, water conservation and filtration, Phytroremediation, Carbon Reduction and Biodiversity / Environmental Biodiversity

findings.antecedent: Biophilic design elements (natural ventilation, lighting, connection to natural environment via openings/surfaces)
findings.consequent: Comfort (thermal, visual, acoustic), restoration, well-being (reduced stress, enhanced cognitive performance, improved mood/emotion)
findings.mechanism: Providing fresh air, daylight, indoor plants, and good landscape supports psychological and biological comfort, allowing for stress reduction, cognitive enhancement, and positive emotional states.
findings.quote: The Biophilic design achieves comfort for the inhabitants of buildings in addition to restorative and Well-Being methods by providing its elements of natural ventilation and natural lighting and the connection to the natural environment through openings and surfaces that allow the supply of fresh air and allow communication with the outside, achieving the psychological and biological comfort of man.

findings.antecedent: Biophilic Urbanism (integrating nature into urban areas at regional, city, neighborhood, building scales)
findings.consequent: Regular experiences with nature, useful nature, peaceful and happy life for people
findings.mechanism: Making nature easily accessible and ensuring close daily contact for all people, thereby supporting human well-being and urban viability.
findings.quote: All the elements of Biophilic are used at the level of regions, cites, neighborhoods, and building [35] to reach the natural, easily accessible, close daily contact and for all the people to achieve a peaceful and happy life.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Architectural designs incorporating biomimetic principles for energy and water conservation will demonstrate measurable reductions in resource consumption compared to conventional designs.

Buildings integrating biophilic design elements will show improved occupant health markers (e.g., lower cortisol, higher HRV) and cognitive performance (e.g., attention, productivity) compared to buildings without such elements.
Urban areas implementing Biophilic Urbanism strategies will exhibit higher levels of perceived restorativeness and environmental satisfaction among residents.
The durability and maintenance requirements of materials inspired by biomimicry will be superior to those of traditional building materials.
The presence of green infrastructure (green roofs, walls, trees) in urban environments will correlate with increased biodiversity and measurable improvements in local air and water quality.
bridge_warrants: The framework explicitly links to the concept of 'restorative environments' (ART, SRT) by emphasizing the therapeutic benefits and positive effects of nature exposure on human health and well-being.
It directly incorporates 'Biophilia' as the underlying biological attractiveness of humans to nature, explaining the benefits of biophilic design.
The principles of 'resource efficiency' and 'life cycle design' are connected to biomimetic strategies, implying a link to ecological engineering and sustainable development theories.
The 'humane design' principle is directly addressed by biophilic design's focus on human health and well-being, aligning with human-centered design approaches.
model_structure: The proposed conceptual framework (Figure 1) is structured hierarchically. At the top are the 'Principles of Sustainable architectural design' (Resource efficiency, Life Cycle Design, Humane Design). These principles are achieved through two main 'Natural strategies': 'Natural-inspired design strategies (Biomimetic Design)' and 'Natural into the built-environment strategies (Biophilic Design)'. Each strategy is further broken down into specific 'Natural Methods' for various aspects (e.g., Energy conservation, Water conservation, Preserving materials, Environmental Protection, Human wellbeing, Urban Design and Planning). The framework visually connects Biomimetic Design to 'Mimics the relationship of the living organism with the environment, society and its features' and Biophilic Design to 'restorative environments'.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Humans have an innate tendency to connect with nature and other living systems, leading to positive psychological and physiological outcomes.
Sustainable solutions can be achieved by emulating nature's designs and processes.

mechanism_chain.description: The framework proposes that integrating biomimetic and biophilic design principles in architecture leads to sustainable outcomes by fostering human-nature connection, improving well-being, and optimizing resource efficiency.

steps.to_construct: Optimized Resource Efficiency and Ecological Performance

steps.from_construct: Improved Human Well-being and Optimized Resource Efficiency
